questions.q: What are the three specific reasons this lesson gives for why a human-executed runbook is unreliable under real 3 a.m. pressure?
options: Detection is slow, execution is error-prone under fatigue and adrenaline, and the runbook itself tends to be stale
Runbooks are illegal to execute without a change-management ticket, humans type too slowly, and DNS always takes exactly ten minutes
Humans are categorically less intelligent than automated systems and should never be trusted with any operational task
Runbooks are always written in the wrong programming language for the on-call engineer's skill set
questions.explain: The lesson names detection speed, fatigue/adrenaline-driven execution errors, and runbook staleness as the three structural problems with relying on a human under pressure.

questions.q: Why does health-check-triggered failover require multiple independent signals to agree rather than a single health check?
options: A single flaky check could trigger an unnecessary failover on a transient blip that would have resolved on its own — this is the flapping problem the design has to guard against
Cloud providers charge extra for using only one health check
Multiple signals are required only for Tier 3 workloads, never for Tier 0
A single health check cannot technically be configured in any monitoring system
questions.explain: Requiring several independent, consecutive signals to agree before triggering protects against flapping — failing over unnecessarily because of a transient condition rather than a real, sustained outage.

questions.q: What does "runbook-as-code" mean in the context of automated failover?
options: Storing the runbook as a PDF in a version-controlled repository instead of a wiki page
The actual recovery procedure is written as tested, executable code that performs the steps directly, rather than a document a human reads and interprets
Writing the runbook in a programming language purely so it looks more technical to auditors
Replacing the on-call engineer's laptop with a different operating system
questions.explain: Runbook-as-code turns the procedure itself — promoting a standby, repointing DNS, scaling up, verifying dependencies — into executable code that runs identically every time, including during drills, rather than a document someone interprets under pressure.

questions.q: Why does runbook-as-code avoid the staleness problem that affects a traditional written runbook?
options: Because code is run and exercised during every drill, so if it's broken, a drill finds out instead of the next real disaster discovering it
Because code never needs to be updated once it is written, unlike documentation
Because code automatically rewrites itself whenever infrastructure changes
Staleness is not actually a concern for executable code of any kind
questions.explain: Because the code actually executes during drills (and in production when triggered), problems surface the same way a real test would surface them — unlike an unexecuted document, which can silently describe a system that no longer exists.

questions.q: According to this lesson, where do humans still have a legitimate role in a well-automated DR posture?
options: Nowhere — full automation should remove humans from every DR tier without exception
Only in writing the original runbook before it is converted to code, after which they have no further role
Lower tiers can route through a human approval step, and every automated path should still have a manual override, or kill switch
Humans should manually execute every failover regardless of tier, since automation is never trustworthy
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that lower-tier workloads with more time can reasonably keep a human approval step, and that every automated path needs a kill switch so a human can intervene if automation makes things worse.
